records.source: Κατήντησεν δὲ καὶ εἰς Δέρβην καὶ εἰς Λύστραν.
records.gloss: He came down then also to Derbe and to Lystra.
pieces: Paul came to Derbe and then on to Lystra.

L.1: And he came also to Derbe and to Lystra.

R.1: Paul traveled to the town of Derbe and then to Lystra.

decisions.choice: he: Paul, travelling with Silas
decisions.reason: The verb is singular and follows 15:40-41, where Paul chooses Silas and goes through Syria and Cilicia. Paul is the leader, so the story follows him.

decisions.choice: Derbe and Lystra: towns of Lycaonia that Paul had visited before
decisions.reason: Paul and Barnabas preached in both towns on their first journey (14:6-21). Coming overland from Cilicia, a traveler reaches Derbe first, which is why the order is the reverse of chapter 14.

decisions.choice: Paul
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject, which the Greek leaves to the context.

decisions.choice: the town of
decisions.reason: Readable says what Derbe was.

records.heading: Timothy joins Paul and Silas

records.source: καὶ ἰδοὺ μαθητής τις ἦν ἐκεῖ ὀνόματι Τιμόθεος, υἱὸς γυναικὸς Ἰουδαίας πιστῆς, πατρὸς δὲ Ἕλληνος, ὃς ἐμαρτυρεῖτο ὑπὸ τῶν ἐν Λύστροις καὶ Ἰκονίῳ ἀδελφῶν·
records.gloss: And behold a disciple certain was there by name Timothy, son of a woman Jewish believing, of a father but Greek, \v 2 who was being well spoken of by the in Lystra and Iconium brothers;
pieces: A disciple called Timothy was living there. His mother was a Jewish woman who believed, but his father was a Greek.
The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} in Lystra and Iconium thought highly of him.

L.1: And look, a certain disciple was there named Timothy, [the] son of a believing Jewish woman, but of a Greek father,
L.2: who was well spoken of by the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} in Lystra and Iconium.

R.1: A follower of Jesus named Timothy lived there. His mother was Jewish, and she believed in Jesus. But his father was not Jewish. He was a Greek.
R.2: The {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} in Lystra and Iconium said good things about Timothy.

decisions.choice: there: most likely Lystra
decisions.reason: Lystra is the last place named, and the believers who speak well of Timothy are those of Lystra and Iconium (16:2). Paul later recalls his sufferings at Lystra, which Timothy knew about (2 Timothy 3:11).

decisions.choice: a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father: a mixed family
decisions.reason: A Greek here means a Gentile, not necessarily someone from Greece. Timothy's mother and grandmother, Eunice and Lois, taught him the Scriptures from childhood (2 Timothy 1:5, 3:15). The father is never said to have believed.

decisions.choice: well spoken of: known and approved by others
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of the seven in 6:3: other people vouch for him.

decisions.choice: brothers: the believers, men and women
decisions.reason: The word is used for the whole community of believers in those towns.

decisions.choice: look
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the word that calls attention to what follows, in current wording rather than an old one.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word takes in all the believers, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: she believed in Jesus
decisions.reason: Readable says what she believed: she was a disciple, like her son.

records.source: τοῦτον ἠθέλησεν ὁ Παῦλος σὺν αὐτῷ ἐξελθεῖν, καὶ λαβὼν περιέτεμεν αὐτὸν διὰ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους τοὺς ὄντας ἐν τοῖς τόποις ἐκείνοις, ᾔδεισαν γὰρ ἅπαντες ὅτι Ἕλλην ὁ πατὴρ αὐτοῦ ὑπῆρχεν.
records.gloss: This one wanted the Paul with him to go forth, and having taken he circumcised him because of the Jews the being in the places those; they knew for all that a Greek the father of him was.
pieces: Paul wanted to have Timothy with him when he set out. With the Jews of that area in mind, he took him and circumcised him, since all of them knew that his father was a Greek.

L.3: Paul wanted this one to go out with him, and taking [him], he circumcised him because of the Jews who were in those places, for they all knew that his father was a Greek.

R.3: Paul wanted Timothy to travel with him. The Jews who lived there all knew that Timothy's father was a Greek. So Paul circumcised Timothy, so that those Jews would not have a reason to refuse to listen to them.

decisions.choice: circumcised: given the sign of God's covenant with Abraham's family
decisions.reason: God gave circumcision to Abraham and his descendants as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17:10-14). Every Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day (Luke 1:59, 2:21). With a Gentile father, Timothy had not been.

decisions.choice: because of the Jews: Timothy, with a Jewish mother, would be seen by them as a Jew who had not kept the law
alternatives: they would see him only as a Gentile
decisions.reason: Everyone knew his father was a Greek, so everyone knew he was uncircumcised. Whether a child of a Jewish mother was then counted a Jew is not certain; the later rabbinic rule says so, but how far it held in Paul's day is unclear. Either way, an uncircumcised companion with a Jewish mother would have closed synagogue doors to Paul.

decisions.choice: not a condition of salvation: done so that the message could be heard
alternatives: Paul going back on the Jerusalem decision
decisions.reason: The Jerusalem meeting had just decided that Gentiles need not be circumcised to be saved (15:1-29), and Paul refused to have Titus, a Greek, circumcised (Galatians 2:3). Timothy's case is different because of his Jewish mother, and Paul says he became like a Jew to win Jews (1 Corinthians 9:20).

decisions.choice: with the Jews of that area in mind
alternatives: because of the Jews who were in those places
decisions.reason: Balanced brings the reason forward, so that the sentence does not end on the reason for the reason.

decisions.choice: so that those Jews would not have a reason to refuse to listen to them
decisions.reason: Readable spells out why the Jews mattered, as the meaning notes explain. The text itself gives only "because of the Jews".

records.source: ὡς δὲ διεπορεύοντο τὰς πόλεις, παρεδίδοσαν αὐτοῖς φυλάσσειν τὰ δόγματα τὰ κεκριμένα ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων καὶ πρεσβυτέρων τῶν ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις.
records.gloss: As then they were passing through the cities, they were delivering to them to keep the decrees the having been decided by the apostles and elders the in Jerusalem.
pieces: As they made their way from town to town, they passed on to the believers the decisions reached by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem, for them to observe.

L.4: And as they went through the cities, they delivered to them the decrees decided on by the apostles and elders who were in Jerusalem, for [them] to keep.

R.4: They traveled from town to town. In each place they told the believers what the apostles and elders in Jerusalem had decided, and they told them to obey these rules.

decisions.choice: decrees: the formal decisions of the Jerusalem meeting
decisions.reason: The word is used for official decisions and decrees (Luke 2:1). Here it means the ruling of 15:28-29: Gentile believers should keep away from food offered to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from sexual immorality.

decisions.choice: to them: the believers in the cities
decisions.reason: The letter of 15:23 was addressed to Gentile believers, and 16:5 goes on to speak of the churches.

decisions.choice: went through, delivered: something they did again and again
decisions.reason: Both verbs are imperfect, for repeated action: in each town they did the same.

decisions.choice: the believers
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the people meant, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: αἱ μὲν οὖν ἐκκλησίαι ἐστερεοῦντο τῇ πίστει καὶ ἐπερίσσευον τῷ ἀριθμῷ καθ’ ἡμέραν.
records.gloss: The indeed therefore churches were being strengthened in the faith and were increasing in the number every day.
pieces: So the churches grew firmer in the faith, and their numbers rose day by day.

L.5: So the churches were being strengthened in the faith and were increasing in number every day.

R.5: So the churches grew stronger in their faith, and more people joined them every day.

decisions.choice: the faith: the believers' trust in Jesus, held in common
decisions.reason: The word has the article, as in 6:7 and 14:22, where it is the faith shared by all who believe. Its first sense is trust; the article does not turn it into a list of doctrines.

decisions.choice: so: a summary that closes a section
alternatives: the result of the decrees only
decisions.reason: Luke marks the end of a stage of the story with a short report of growth, as in 6:7, 9:31 and 12:24.

decisions.choice: more people joined them
decisions.reason: Readable says what the growth in number meant.

records.source: Διῆλθον δὲ τὴν Φρυγίαν καὶ Γαλατικὴν χώραν, κωλυθέντες ὑπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος λαλῆσαι τὸν λόγον ἐν τῇ Ἀσίᾳ, ἐλθόντες δὲ κατὰ τὴν Μυσίαν ἐπείραζον εἰς τὴν Βιθυνίαν πορευθῆναι καὶ οὐκ εἴασεν αὐτοὺς τὸ πνεῦμα Ἰησοῦ·
records.gloss: They passed through then the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in the Asia; \v 7 having come then to the Mysia they were trying into the Bithynia to go, and not allowed them the Spirit of Jesus;
pieces: They went on through the Phrygian and Galatian country, because the Holy Spirit had stopped them from speaking the word in Asia.
Coming as far as Mysia, they made an attempt to go on into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit it.

L.6: And they went through the Phrygian and Galatian region, having been forbidden by the Holy Spirit to speak the word in Asia.
L.7: And when they came up to Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, and the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.

R.6: Then they went through the area of Phrygia and Galatia. The Holy Spirit did not let them tell God's message in the province of Asia.
R.7: When they came near Mysia, they tried to go north into Bithynia. But the Spirit of Jesus did not let them go there.

decisions.choice: the Phrygian and Galatian region: one area that was both Phrygian and Galatian
alternatives: two areas, Phrygia and the region of Galatia
decisions.reason: One article governs both words, and Phrygian can be an adjective, which suggests a single area: the part of Phrygia that lay in the Roman province of Galatia, where Iconium and Pisidian Antioch were. The words can also be read as two areas.

decisions.choice: Asia: the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey
decisions.reason: Its chief city was Ephesus. Paul worked there later for over two years (19:1-10).

decisions.choice: having been forbidden: the Spirit's leading came before or during this stage of the journey
alternatives: the reason they went to Phrygia, stated as a fact
decisions.reason: The participle is aorist. It may tell why they took this route, or what happened on it. Luke does not say how the Spirit spoke, whether through a prophet, a vision or events.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of Jesus: the Holy Spirit, who is also the Spirit of Jesus
decisions.reason: The same Spirit is named in 16:6 and 16:7. Only here is he called the Spirit of Jesus; compare "the Spirit of Christ" (Romans 8:9), "the Spirit of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:19) and "the Spirit of his Son" (Galatians 4:6). The risen Jesus pours out the Spirit (2:33) and leads his people by him.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "the Spirit of Jesus"
alternatives: some later manuscripts read only "the Spirit"
decisions.reason: The early manuscripts have "the Spirit of Jesus"; later ones, followed by the King James Version, leave out "of Jesus". Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: came up to Mysia: reached its border
decisions.reason: The preposition means opposite or over against. They came to the edge of Mysia, in the northwest, and tried to turn northeast.

decisions.choice: the province of Asia; go north
decisions.reason: Readable says that Asia was a province, not the continent, and which way Bithynia lay.

decisions.choice: tell God's message
decisions.reason: Readable says what the word was, as at 6:2.

records.heading: The call from Macedonia

records.source: παρελθόντες δὲ τὴν Μυσίαν κατέβησαν εἰς Τρῳάδα.
records.gloss: Having passed by then the Mysia they came down to Troas.
pieces: So they skirted Mysia and went down to Troas.

L.8: And passing by Mysia, they came down to Troas.

R.8: So they went along the edge of Mysia and came down to the city of Troas, on the coast.

decisions.choice: passing by: going through without stopping to preach
decisions.reason: Troas itself lay in Mysia, so they must have crossed it. The verb means they did not stay or work there.

decisions.choice: Troas: a port on the Aegean coast, near ancient Troy
decisions.reason: Alexandria Troas was a Roman colony and the usual port for sailing from Asia to Macedonia. Paul passed through it again (20:5-12; 2 Corinthians 2:12).

decisions.choice: the city of; on the coast
decisions.reason: Readable says what Troas was, since the next step is a sea voyage.

records.source: καὶ ὅραμα διὰ νυκτὸς τῷ Παύλῳ ὤφθη, ἀνὴρ Μακεδών τις ἦν ἑστὼς καὶ παρακαλῶν αὐτὸν καὶ λέγων· Διαβὰς εἰς Μακεδονίαν βοήθησον ἡμῖν.
records.gloss: And a vision during night to the Paul appeared: a man Macedonian certain was standing and urging him and saying, Having crossed over into Macedonia help us.
pieces: In the night Paul saw a vision. A man of Macedonia stood there and pleaded with him, "Cross over to Macedonia and help us!"

L.9: And a vision appeared to Paul during [the] night: a certain Macedonian man was standing and urging him and saying, "Cross over into Macedonia [and] help us."

R.9: That night God showed Paul a vision. In it a man from Macedonia was standing and begging him, "Come across the sea to Macedonia and help us!"

decisions.choice: a vision: something seen that God sends
decisions.reason: Luke uses the word for the visions by which God guided Ananias (9:10), Cornelius (10:3), Peter (10:17) and Paul again at Corinth (18:9).

decisions.choice: Macedonia: the Roman province north of Greece, across the Aegean Sea
decisions.reason: Its cities included Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea, where the next chapters go. The text does not say how Paul knew that the man was a Macedonian; his words make it plain.

decisions.choice: help us: the help is the gospel
alternatives: help in a war or a famine
decisions.reason: Paul and the others take the call as God's call to bring the gospel there (16:10).

decisions.choice: God showed Paul a vision
decisions.reason: Readable says who sent the vision, as the meaning note and 16:10 explain.

decisions.choice: come across the sea
decisions.reason: Readable says what lay between Troas and Macedonia.

records.source: ὡς δὲ τὸ ὅραμα εἶδεν, εὐθέως ἐζητήσαμεν ἐξελθεῖν εἰς Μακεδονίαν, συμβιβάζοντες ὅτι προσκέκληται ἡμᾶς ὁ θεὸς εὐαγγελίσασθαι αὐτούς.
records.gloss: When then the vision he saw, immediately we sought to go forth into Macedonia, concluding that has called us the God to preach the gospel to them.
pieces: As soon as he had seen the vision, we looked for a way to set out for Macedonia, sure now that God had called us to bring the gospel to its people.

L.10: And when he had seen the vision, immediately we sought to go out into Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to preach the gospel to them.

R.10: After Paul saw the vision, we started at once to look for a way to get to Macedonia. We were sure that God was calling us to tell the people there the good news.

decisions.choice: we: the narrator now counts himself among Paul's companions
alternatives: the narrator copies another person's diary
a style of storytelling with no real narrator present
decisions.reason: Up to here the story speaks of "they". From this sentence the narrator says "we", and he does so until the arrest at Philippi (16:17), and again from Philippi onward (20:5-21:18; 27:1-28:16). He was present for these events. The text never names him; who he was is a question for the book as a whole, and the translation does not settle it.

decisions.choice: concluding: reasoning it out together from the vision
decisions.reason: The verb means to put things together and draw a conclusion. The vision called; they understood it as God's call.

decisions.choice: to them: the people of Macedonia
alternatives: the man of the vision only
decisions.reason: The pronoun refers back to Macedonia, meaning those who live there.

decisions.choice: its people
decisions.reason: Balanced says whom the pronoun means, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: tell the good news
decisions.reason: Readable uses "good news" for the gospel, as everywhere.

records.source: Ἀναχθέντες οὖν ἀπὸ Τρῳάδος εὐθυδρομήσαμεν εἰς Σαμοθρᾴκην, τῇ δὲ ἐπιούσῃ εἰς Νέαν Πόλιν, κἀκεῖθεν εἰς Φιλίππους, ἥτις ἐστὶν πρώτη τῆς μερίδος Μακεδονίας πόλις, κολωνία.
records.gloss: Having set sail therefore from Troas we ran a straight course to Samothrace, the and following [day] to Nea Polis, \v 12 and from there to Philippi, which is a leading of the district of Macedonia city, a colony.
pieces: So we set sail from Troas and ran with a straight course to Samothrace, and the next day reached Neapolis.
From there we made our way to Philippi, which ranks as a leading city of its district of Macedonia and is a Roman colony.

L.11: So setting sail from Troas, we ran a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next [day] to Neapolis,
L.12: and from there to Philippi, which is a leading city of the district of Macedonia, a colony.

R.11: We sailed from Troas straight to the island of Samothrace. The next day we sailed on to the town of Neapolis.
R.12: From there we went to the city of Philippi. It was an important city in that part of Macedonia. It was also a Roman colony, a city that Rome had settled with its own citizens.

decisions.choice: ran a straight course: sailed straight there, with a good wind
decisions.reason: The verb is a sailor's word for a straight run. The voyage took two days; the same trip the other way took five (20:6).

decisions.choice: Samothrace, an island on the way; Neapolis, the port of Philippi
decisions.reason: Samothrace is a mountainous island in the north Aegean, a usual stop overnight. Neapolis is the modern Kavala, about ten miles from Philippi.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "a leading city of the district of Macedonia"
alternatives: "a city of the first district of Macedonia"
decisions.reason: The manuscripts differ in small ways at this point. The SBLGNT follows the reading of most early manuscripts. A reading that changes one letter, "of the first district", is supported by a few Latin manuscripts and is preferred by some editors, because Rome had divided Macedonia into four districts (Livy 45.29) and Philippi lay in the first. Codex Bezae calls Philippi the capital. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: leading: first in rank or importance, not the capital
decisions.reason: Amphipolis was the chief city of Philippi's district, and Thessalonica the capital of the province. Without the article, the word is best read as one of the foremost cities, a title cities used with pride.

decisions.choice: a colony: a Roman colony, a piece of Rome abroad
decisions.reason: After the battle of Philippi in 42 BC, and again after Actium in 31 BC, Rome settled veterans there. A colony was governed by Roman law, with its own Roman magistrates, and its citizens were Roman citizens. This explains the charge of 16:21 and Paul's protest in 16:37.

decisions.choice: the island of; the town of; the city of
decisions.reason: Readable says what each place was.

decisions.choice: Roman colony (B); a city that Rome had settled with its own citizens (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say whose colony it was, and Readable what that meant, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: Neapolis
decisions.reason: The two Greek words, meaning New City, are the town's name, written as one word.

records.heading: Lydia at the place of prayer

records.source: ἦμεν δὲ ἐν ταύτῃ τῇ πόλει διατρίβοντες ἡμέρας τινάς.
records.gloss: We were then in this the city staying days some.
pieces: We spent several days in that city.

L.12: And we were staying in this city some days.

R.12: We stayed in Philippi for several days.

decisions.choice: were staying: a stay of some days before the Sabbath of 16:13
decisions.reason: The words are vague. The stay before the first Sabbath was short; the whole stay was longer (16:18).

decisions.choice: Philippi
decisions.reason: Readable names the city.

records.source: τῇ τε ἡμέρᾳ τῶν σαββάτων ἐξήλθομεν ἔξω τῆς πύλης παρὰ ποταμὸν οὗ ἐνομίζομεν προσευχὴν εἶναι, καὶ καθίσαντες ἐλαλοῦμεν ταῖς συνελθούσαις γυναιξίν.
records.gloss: On the and day of the Sabbaths we went forth outside the gate beside a river where we were supposing a place of prayer to be, and having sat down we were speaking to the having come together women.
pieces: On the Sabbath day we went out beyond the gate, beside a river, where we thought there might be a place of prayer. We took a seat and spoke to the women who had come together.

L.13: And on the Sabbath day we went out outside the gate beside a river, where we supposed there was a place of prayer, and sitting down, we were speaking to the women who had come together.

R.13: On the Sabbath day we went out of the city gate to the river. We thought Jewish people might meet there to pray. We sat down and talked to the women who had come there.

decisions.choice: a place of prayer: a place where Jews met for prayer
decisions.reason: The word means prayer, and was used for a Jewish meeting place, often a building (Josephus, and inscriptions from Egypt). Here it may be an open place by the water. No synagogue is named at Philippi, perhaps because few Jews lived there; only women are mentioned.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "where we supposed there was a place of prayer"
decisions.reason: Manuscripts differ between a form meaning "we supposed" and one meaning "it was customary". The SBLGNT reads the first. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the day of the Sabbaths: the Sabbath day
decisions.reason: The plural is a usual way of naming the Sabbath (Luke 4:16).

decisions.choice: sitting down: the posture of a teacher
decisions.reason: Teachers sat to teach in the synagogue (Luke 4:20).

decisions.choice: Jewish people might meet there to pray
alternatives: there was a place of prayer
decisions.reason: Readable says what a place of prayer was, as the meaning note explains.

records.source: καί τις γυνὴ ὀνόματι Λυδία, πορφυρόπωλις πόλεως Θυατείρων σεβομένη τὸν θεόν, ἤκουεν, ἧς ὁ κύριος διήνοιξεν τὴν καρδίαν προσέχειν τοῖς λαλουμένοις ὑπὸ τοῦ Παύλου.
records.gloss: And a certain woman by name Lydia, a seller of purple of a city of Thyatira, worshiping the God, was listening, of whom the Lord opened the heart to pay attention to the things being spoken by the Paul.
pieces: A woman named Lydia was listening, a dealer in purple cloth from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God. The Lord opened her heart to heed what Paul was saying.

L.14: And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple [cloth] from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God, was listening; the Lord opened her heart to pay attention to the things spoken by Paul.

R.14: A woman named Lydia was there listening. She was from the city of Thyatira, and she sold costly purple cloth. She was not a Jew, but she worshiped the God of Israel. The Lord opened her heart, so that she paid close attention to what Paul said.

decisions.choice: a seller of purple: a trader in cloth dyed purple
decisions.reason: Purple dye was costly, and purple cloth was worn by the wealthy. Thyatira, in the region of Lydia in Asia, was known for its dyers, as inscriptions from the city show. A trader in such goods was likely a woman of some means; she has a house large enough for guests (16:15).

decisions.choice: who worshiped God: a Gentile who worshiped the God of Israel
decisions.reason: Luke uses this phrase and "those who fear God" for Gentiles who joined in Jewish worship without becoming Jews, like Cornelius (10:2) and some in Thessalonica and Corinth (17:4, 18:7). She was with the Jewish women at prayer.

decisions.choice: the Lord opened her heart: God's work brought her to faith
decisions.reason: The risen Jesus opened the minds of the disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). The heart stands for mind and will. Her listening was real, and the Lord made it fruitful. "The Lord" may be Jesus or God; Luke often leaves it open.

decisions.choice: pay attention to: take to heart and respond
decisions.reason: The verb means to give heed to something, and act on it, as in 8:6.

decisions.choice: she was not a Jew, but she worshiped the God of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable says what the phrase implied, as the meaning note explains. It is not certain that she was not Jewish.

decisions.choice: costly
decisions.reason: Readable says why purple cloth mattered.

records.source: ὡς δὲ ἐβαπτίσθη καὶ ὁ οἶκος αὐτῆς, παρεκάλεσεν λέγουσα· Εἰ κεκρίκατέ με πιστὴν τῷ κυρίῳ εἶναι, εἰσελθόντες εἰς τὸν οἶκόν μου μένετε· καὶ παρεβιάσατο ἡμᾶς.
records.gloss: When then she was baptized and the household of her, she urged saying, If you have judged me faithful to the Lord to be, having come into the house of me stay; and she prevailed upon us.
pieces: After she and her household had been baptized, she pressed us to accept her offer: "If you are satisfied that I am faithful to the Lord, come into my home and stay." And she would not take no for an answer.

L.15: And when she and her household were baptized, she urged [us], saying, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house [and] stay." And she prevailed upon us.

R.15: Lydia and the people in her home were baptized. Then she begged us, "If you agree that I truly trust in the Lord, come and stay in my house." She kept asking until we agreed.

decisions.choice: her household: those who lived under her roof, family and servants
decisions.reason: A household took in relatives, slaves and others who lived in the house. No husband is named, so she seems to have been its head. The text does not say whether there were children, or how old they were.

decisions.choice: faithful to the Lord: a true believer in the Lord
decisions.reason: The word can mean believing or trustworthy. Here it is the result of her baptism: she asks them to accept that she truly belongs to the Lord.

decisions.choice: prevailed upon: urged them until they gave in
decisions.reason: The same verb is used of the two disciples urging Jesus to stay at Emmaus (Luke 24:29).

decisions.choice: she would not take no for an answer
decisions.reason: Balanced puts the verb's sense of pressing until the other side yields into everyday words.

decisions.choice: truly trust in
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense chosen in the meaning note.

records.source: Ἐγένετο δὲ πορευομένων ἡμῶν εἰς τὴν προσευχὴν παιδίσκην τινὰ ἔχουσαν πνεῦμα πύθωνα ὑπαντῆσαι ἡμῖν, ἥτις ἐργασίαν πολλὴν παρεῖχεν τοῖς κυρίοις αὐτῆς μαντευομένη·
records.gloss: It happened then, going of us to the place of prayer, a slave girl certain having a spirit, a python, met us, who profit much was bringing to the masters of her by fortune-telling.
pieces: Once, on our way to the place of prayer, a slave girl came to meet us who had a soothsaying spirit. Her fortune-telling brought in a large income for her masters.

L.16: And it happened, as we were going to the place of prayer, [that] a certain slave girl having a spirit of Python met us, who brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling.

R.16: One day we were going to the place of prayer. A slave girl met us who had a spirit in her that let her tell people what would happen in the future. Her owners made a lot of money from her fortune-telling.

decisions.choice: a spirit of Python: a spirit that gave oracles, as people believed the god of Delphi did
decisions.reason: Python was the serpent of Greek myth that guarded Delphi, the most famous oracle of the Greek world, before Apollo killed it. The name came to be used for a spirit that spoke through someone to foretell things, and for the people it spoke through; Plutarch uses it of those who spoke in a trance. People in Philippi would have taken the girl to be inspired by Apollo.

decisions.choice: a spirit: a real spirit, which Paul drives out
decisions.reason: Paul speaks to the spirit and it comes out (16:18), as unclean spirits do at Jesus's command (Luke 4:33-35). Luke does not call it unclean, but he treats it as opposed to God's work.

decisions.choice: fortune-telling: pagan divination
decisions.reason: This verb is used in the Greek Old Testament for the divination God forbids (Deuteronomy 18:10; 1 Samuel 28:8), never for the prophets of the Lord.

decisions.choice: a slave girl and her masters: she was owned, perhaps by partners
decisions.reason: Her owners, more than one, profited from her powers, as owners of a skilled slave would.

decisions.choice: a soothsaying spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced says what the name meant to its hearers; Literal keeps the name, which the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: a spirit in her that let her tell people what would happen in the future
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what the spirit did.

decisions.choice: slave girl
decisions.reason: "Slave" at every level, as the style guide keeps it for people owned as property: her owners made money from her (m4).

records.heading: A slave girl with a spirit of Python

records.source: αὕτη κατακολουθοῦσα τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ ἡμῖν ἔκραζεν λέγουσα· Οὗτοι οἱ ἄνθρωποι δοῦλοι τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου εἰσίν, οἵτινες καταγγέλλουσιν ὑμῖν ὁδὸν σωτηρίας.
records.gloss: She following the Paul and us was crying out saying, These the men slaves of the God the Most High are, who proclaim to you a way of salvation.
pieces: She trailed after Paul and the rest of us, crying out, "These men are servants of the Most High God, and they are announcing to you a way of salvation!"

L.17: She, following Paul and us, kept crying out, saying, "These men are slaves of the Most High God, who proclaim to you a way of salvation."

R.17: She followed Paul and the rest of us around and kept shouting, "These men are servants of the Most High God! They are telling you how you can be saved!"

decisions.choice: the Most High God: true in itself, but a title pagans also used for their highest god
decisions.reason: The title goes back to Genesis 14:18-20. Demons cried out to Jesus as "Son of the Most High God" (Luke 8:28). In the Greek world, inscriptions honor Zeus and other gods as "the Most High", so hearers in Philippi might not have known which god was meant.

decisions.choice: a way of salvation: one way among others, as her hearers would take it
decisions.reason: There is no article. Her words are true as far as they go, but in a city of many gods they could sound like one more path. This may be why Paul was troubled (16:18).

decisions.choice: slaves: men wholly owned by God
decisions.reason: The word means a slave. The apostles use it of themselves (Romans 1:1; Philippians 1:1) and of believers in prayer (4:29).

decisions.choice: these men: Paul and his companions
decisions.reason: The word here points to particular men, the missionaries.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "to you"
decisions.reason: The two Greek pronouns sounded alike and were often confused by copyists. "To you" is better attested. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: how you can be saved
decisions.reason: Readable puts the noun as a verb. It keeps the sense of the meaning note, since "how" does not claim it is the only way.

decisions.choice: servants
decisions.reason: "Servant" in Balanced and Readable, as the style guide has it; the meaning decision (m3) keeps that the person was owned, and Literal keeps "slave".

records.source: τοῦτο δὲ ἐποίει ἐπὶ πολλὰς ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: This then she was doing for many days.
pieces: She kept this up for many days.

L.18: And she was doing this for many days.

R.18: She did this day after day for a long time.

decisions.choice: was doing: again and again
decisions.reason: The imperfect shows that it went on day after day.

records.source: διαπονηθεὶς δὲ Παῦλος καὶ ἐπιστρέψας τῷ πνεύματι εἶπεν· Παραγγέλλω σοι ἐν ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ ἐξελθεῖν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς· καὶ ἐξῆλθεν αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ.
records.gloss: Having been greatly troubled then Paul and having turned to the spirit said, I command you in name of Jesus Christ to come out from her; and it came out in the same hour.
pieces: In the end Paul grew weary and vexed. He turned and told the spirit, "I order you in the name of Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}} to come out of her!" It came out that same hour.

L.18: But Paul, greatly troubled, turned and said to the spirit, "I command you in [the] name of Jesus {{christos:Christ|Messiah}} to come out of her." And it came out that very hour.

R.18: Paul became very upset. He turned around and said to the spirit, "By the power of Jesus {{christos:Christ|the Messiah}}, I order you to come out of her!" At once the spirit left her.

decisions.choice: greatly troubled: annoyed and worn down
decisions.reason: The verb means to be deeply disturbed or exasperated; the leaders were so with the apostles in 4:2. Luke does not say why: perhaps the noise, perhaps that a pagan spirit was announcing the message and confusing it.

decisions.choice: in the name of Jesus Christ: by his authority and power
decisions.reason: As in 3:6 and 3:16, the name stands for the person. In 19:13-16 those who use the name like a spell are overpowered.

decisions.choice: that very hour: at once
decisions.reason: An hour often means simply the moment (Luke 2:38, 7:21).

decisions.choice: by the power of
decisions.reason: Readable says what the name means here, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: in the end
decisions.reason: Balanced shows that his patience ran out after many days (16:18).

records.source: Ἰδόντες δὲ οἱ κύριοι αὐτῆς ὅτι ἐξῆλθεν ἡ ἐλπὶς τῆς ἐργασίας αὐτῶν ἐπιλαβόμενοι τὸν Παῦλον καὶ τὸν Σιλᾶν εἵλκυσαν εἰς τὴν ἀγορὰν ἐπὶ τοὺς ἄρχοντας, καὶ προσαγαγόντες αὐτοὺς τοῖς στρατηγοῖς εἶπαν· Οὗτοι οἱ ἄνθρωποι ἐκταράσσουσιν ἡμῶν τὴν πόλιν Ἰουδαῖοι ὑπάρχοντες, καὶ καταγγέλλουσιν ἔθη ἃ οὐκ ἔξεστιν ἡμῖν παραδέχεσθαι οὐδὲ ποιεῖν Ῥωμαίοις οὖσιν.
records.gloss: Having seen then the masters of her that went out the hope of the profit of them, having seized the Paul and the Silas they dragged [them] into the marketplace before the rulers, \v 20 and having brought them to the magistrates they said, These the men are throwing into confusion our the city, Jews being, \v 21 and they proclaim customs which not it is lawful for us to accept nor to practice, Romans being.
pieces: Her masters saw that their hope of gain had gone out of her along with the spirit. So they laid hold of Paul and Silas and hauled them off to the rulers in the marketplace.
Bringing them before the magistrates, they said, "These men are upsetting our whole city. They are Jews,
and they preach customs that we cannot lawfully take up or follow, since we are Romans."

L.19: But when her masters saw that the hope of their profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged [them] into the marketplace before the rulers,
L.20: and bringing them to the magistrates, they said, "These men are throwing our city into confusion, being Jews,
L.21: and they proclaim customs that it is not lawful for us to accept or to practice, being Romans."

R.19: The girl's owners saw that she could no longer make money for them. So they grabbed Paul and Silas and dragged them to the city leaders in the marketplace.
R.20: They brought them to the chief officials of the city and said, "These men are Jews, and they are causing a lot of trouble in our city.
R.21: They are teaching customs that we Romans are not allowed to accept or follow."

decisions.choice: gone out: the same verb as for the spirit coming out
decisions.reason: The spirit "came out" (16:18) and the owners' hope of profit "went out" with it. The repeated verb makes a grim joke.

decisions.choice: rulers and magistrates: the same men, the chief officials of the colony
decisions.reason: "Rulers" is a general word for those in authority. "Magistrates" renders the Greek word for generals, which was used in Greek cities for the two chief officials who ran a Roman colony, known in Latin as duumvirs or praetors. Luke uses the word only of these officials from here on (16:22, 35, 36, 38).

decisions.choice: the marketplace: the forum, the city's public square
decisions.reason: The forum held the courts and offices of the city's officials. The foundations of the forum of Roman Philippi can still be seen.

decisions.choice: being Jews: an appeal to feeling against Jews
decisions.reason: The owners say nothing of their lost income. They set "Jews" against "Romans" (16:21). About this time the emperor Claudius ordered Jews out of Rome (18:2).

decisions.choice: customs not lawful for Romans: foreign religious ways that Romans should not take up
decisions.reason: Romans held that citizens should not adopt foreign cults that were not approved. The charge is vague, but it was serious in a colony that prided itself on being Roman.

decisions.choice: out of her along with the spirit
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the wordplay of the meaning note by saying what went out with what.

decisions.choice: the chief officials of the city
decisions.reason: Readable describes the office instead of naming it, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: she could no longer make money for them
alternatives: the hope of their profit had gone out
decisions.reason: Readable says what the loss was; the wordplay cannot be kept in plain words.

records.source: καὶ συνεπέστη ὁ ὄχλος κατ’ αὐτῶν, καὶ οἱ στρατηγοὶ περιρήξαντες αὐτῶν τὰ ἱμάτια ἐκέλευον ῥαβδίζειν, πολλάς τε ἐπιθέντες αὐτοῖς πληγὰς ἔβαλον εἰς φυλακήν, παραγγείλαντες τῷ δεσμοφύλακι ἀσφαλῶς τηρεῖν αὐτούς·
records.gloss: And rose up together the crowd against them, and the magistrates having torn off of them the garments were ordering to beat with rods, \v 23 many and having laid on them blows they threw [them] into prison, having commanded the jailer securely to keep them;
pieces: The crowd too rose up against them, and the magistrates tore the clothes off them and ordered them beaten with rods.
When they had struck them many blows, they threw them into prison and told the jailer to keep them safely locked up.

L.22: And the crowd rose up together against them, and the magistrates, tearing off their garments, ordered [them] to be beaten with rods,
L.23: and after laying many blows on them, they threw [them] into prison, commanding the jailer to guard them securely.

R.22: A crowd of people joined in and turned against Paul and Silas. The city officials had their clothes torn off and ordered men to beat them with wooden rods.
R.23: They beat Paul and Silas many times. Then they threw them into prison and told the jailer to keep them locked up tight.

decisions.choice: tearing off their garments: stripping Paul and Silas for the beating
alternatives: the magistrates tearing their own robes in outrage
decisions.reason: The pronoun could refer to the magistrates, but a Roman beating was given on the bare back, and the magistrates order it at once. The officials gave the order; their attendants did the stripping.

decisions.choice: beaten with rods: the Roman punishment carried out by the magistrates' attendants
decisions.reason: The attendants of Roman magistrates, the lictors, carried bundles of rods (16:35). Paul says he was beaten with rods three times (2 Corinthians 11:25) and speaks of being shamefully treated at Philippi (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

decisions.choice: guard them securely: keep them so they could not escape
decisions.reason: The adverb means safely or surely; the next verse shows what the jailer did to make sure.

decisions.choice: ordered men to beat them with wooden rods
alternatives: ordered them to be beaten with rods
decisions.reason: Readable says that others carried out the beating, and what the rods were.

records.source: ὃς παραγγελίαν τοιαύτην λαβὼν ἔβαλεν αὐτοὺς εἰς τὴν ἐσωτέραν φυλακὴν καὶ τοὺς πόδας ἠσφαλίσατο αὐτῶν εἰς τὸ ξύλον.
records.gloss: who an order such having received threw them into the inner prison and the feet fastened of them in the wood.
pieces: Given such a charge, the jailer threw them into the inner part of the prison and made their feet fast in the stocks.

L.24: Having received such an order, he threw them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.

R.24: Because of this order, the jailer put them in a room deep inside the prison. He locked their feet between heavy blocks of wood so they could not move.

decisions.choice: the stocks: a wooden frame that held the feet fast
decisions.reason: The word means wood. Stocks had holes for the legs and could be set to spread them painfully apart. With their backs torn from the beating, the prisoners could neither move nor lie easily.

decisions.choice: the inner prison: the innermost, most secure cell
decisions.reason: The jailer chose the place hardest to escape from, as ordered (16:23).

decisions.choice: between heavy blocks of wood so they could not move
decisions.reason: Readable describes the stocks.

decisions.choice: the jailer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the subject; the Greek joins this to the last sentence with "who".

records.source: Κατὰ δὲ τὸ μεσονύκτιον Παῦλος καὶ Σιλᾶς προσευχόμενοι ὕμνουν τὸν θεόν, ἐπηκροῶντο δὲ αὐτῶν οἱ δέσμιοι·
records.gloss: About then the midnight Paul and Silas praying were singing hymns to the God, were listening and to them the prisoners.
pieces: At midnight, as Paul and Silas prayed, they sang praises to God, and the prisoners listened.

L.25: And about midnight Paul and Silas, praying, were singing hymns to God, and the prisoners were listening to them.

R.25: Around midnight Paul and Silas prayed and sang songs to praise God. The other prisoners in the jail heard them.

decisions.choice: praying, singing hymns: prayer that took the form of song
decisions.reason: The participle and the verb go together: their prayer was sung praise, as in many Psalms.

decisions.choice: singing hymns: singing praise to God
decisions.reason: The verb is used of Jesus and the disciples singing after the last supper (Mark 14:26), probably Psalms.

decisions.choice: were listening: listening closely
decisions.reason: The verb means to listen attentively, as to a performance.

decisions.choice: the other prisoners in the jail
decisions.reason: Readable makes clear that these were the others held there.

records.heading: Midnight in the prison at Philippi

records.source: ἄφνω δὲ σεισμὸς ἐγένετο μέγας ὥστε σαλευθῆναι τὰ θεμέλια τοῦ δεσμωτηρίου, ἠνεῴχθησαν δὲ παραχρῆμα αἱ θύραι πᾶσαι, καὶ πάντων τὰ δεσμὰ ἀνέθη.
records.gloss: Suddenly then earthquake happened great so that were shaken the foundations of the prison; were opened then immediately the doors all, and of all the chains were unfastened.
pieces: All at once a great earthquake struck, so strong that the prison was shaken to its foundations. In that instant all the doors came open, and the chains of every prisoner fell loose.

L.26: And suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the foundations of the prison were shaken; and immediately all the doors were opened, and the chains of all were unfastened.

R.26: Suddenly there was a strong earthquake. It shook the prison down to its foundations. Right away all the doors of the prison opened, and the chains fell off all the prisoners.

decisions.choice: the earthquake: God's answer, freeing his servants
decisions.reason: Luke does not say so in words, but God frees his messengers from prison in 5:19 and 12:7-10, and an earthquake follows prayer in 4:31. Even so, Paul and Silas do not run.

decisions.choice: the chains were unfastened: came loose from what held them
decisions.reason: Chains were fixed to the walls or the stocks; the shaking loosened the fastenings.

records.source: ἔξυπνος δὲ γενόμενος ὁ δεσμοφύλαξ καὶ ἰδὼν ἀνεῳγμένας τὰς θύρας τῆς φυλακῆς σπασάμενος τὴν μάχαιραν ἤμελλεν ἑαυτὸν ἀναιρεῖν, νομίζων ἐκπεφευγέναι τοὺς δεσμίους.
records.gloss: Awake then having become the jailer and having seen opened the doors of the prison, having drawn the sword he was about himself to kill, supposing to have escaped the prisoners.
pieces: Startled out of sleep, the jailer saw that the prison doors stood open. Believing that the prisoners had got away, he drew his sword, ready to take his own life.

L.27: And the jailer, waking up and seeing the doors of the prison opened, drew [his] sword and was about to kill himself, supposing that the prisoners had escaped.

R.27: The jailer woke up and saw that the doors of the prison were open. He thought the prisoners had run away. So he pulled out his sword to kill himself.

decisions.choice: about to kill himself: he expected to die for the escape
decisions.reason: A guard who let prisoners escape could suffer the penalty they would have suffered (12:19, 27:42). The jailer chose death by his own hand over trial and disgrace.

decisions.choice: supposing: he assumed it, without looking
decisions.reason: In the dark he saw the open doors and drew the obvious conclusion.

records.source: ἐφώνησεν δὲ φωνῇ μεγάλῃ ὁ Παῦλος λέγων· Μηδὲν πράξῃς σεαυτῷ κακόν, ἅπαντες γάρ ἐσμεν ἐνθάδε.
records.gloss: Called out but with a voice loud the Paul saying, Nothing do to yourself harm, all for we are here.
pieces: But Paul shouted at the top of his voice, "Do not hurt yourself! Every one of us is still here!"

L.28: But Paul called out with a loud voice, saying, "Do yourself no harm, for we are all here."

R.28: But Paul shouted loudly, "Do not hurt yourself! We are all still here!"

decisions.choice: all: all the prisoners, not only Paul and Silas
decisions.reason: The jailer feared that the prisoners had escaped (16:27). Paul tells him none has. Luke does not say why the others stayed.

decisions.choice: do yourself no harm: a command not to go through with it
decisions.reason: The aorist with "no" forbids an act about to be done.

decisions.choice: still here
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out that no one had left.

records.source: αἰτήσας δὲ φῶτα εἰσεπήδησεν καὶ ἔντρομος γενόμενος προσέπεσεν τῷ Παύλῳ καὶ τῷ Σιλᾷ, καὶ προαγαγὼν αὐτοὺς ἔξω ἔφη· Κύριοι, τί με δεῖ ποιεῖν ἵνα σωθῶ;
records.gloss: Having asked for then lights he rushed in, and trembling having become he fell down before the Paul and the Silas, \v 30 and having brought them outside he was saying, Sirs, what me is it necessary to do that I may be saved?
pieces: He called for lights and ran inside, and shaking with fear he fell at the feet of Paul and Silas.
He led them out and said, "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"

L.29: And asking for lights, he rushed in, and becoming terrified, he fell down before Paul and Silas,
L.30: and bringing them outside, he said, "Sirs, what must I do that I may be saved?"

R.29: The jailer asked for lamps and ran into the prison. He was shaking with fear, and he bowed down in front of Paul and Silas.
R.30: Then he brought them outside and asked, "Sirs, what do I need to do to be saved?"

decisions.choice: fell down before: a sign of awe and fear
decisions.reason: He bows before the men he now sees as servants of a powerful God, as Cornelius did before Peter (10:25). They do not refuse it here, but they point him at once to the Lord Jesus (16:31).

decisions.choice: Sirs: a respectful address
decisions.reason: The word is the plural of "lord" and was a polite way to address men of standing. It is the same word used of the slave girl's masters (16:16, 16:19).

decisions.choice: be saved: rescued by God, in the full sense Paul gives it in his answer
decisions.reason: The jailer may have meant more or less than he knew. The slave girl had announced "a way of salvation" (16:17) for days in the city, and the earthquake had shown God's power. Paul and Silas answer with salvation through the Lord Jesus (16:31).

decisions.choice: lamps
decisions.reason: Readable names the kind of light he would have used.

records.source: οἱ δὲ εἶπαν· Πίστευσον ἐπὶ τὸν κύριον Ἰησοῦν, καὶ σωθήσῃ σὺ καὶ ὁ οἶκός σου.
records.gloss: They then said, Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and the household of you.
pieces: They answered, "Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."

L.31: And they said, "Believe on the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household."

R.31: They said, "Believe in the Lord Jesus. Then you will be saved, and so will the people in your home."

decisions.choice: believe on the Lord Jesus: put your trust in him
decisions.reason: The preposition means on or upon: trust that rests on a person. The same phrase is used in 9:42 and 11:17.

decisions.choice: you and your household: the promise is for them too, as they also believe
alternatives: the household is saved by the jailer's faith alone
decisions.reason: The word is spoken to all in the house (16:32), and the household rejoices together with the jailer, who had believed (16:34). The promise reaches them through the same message and faith; compare 11:14, where Cornelius is told he and his household will be saved.

decisions.choice: the Lord Jesus: Jesus as Lord
decisions.reason: The jailer addressed them as "sirs" (16:30); they point him to the one who is Lord.

records.source: καὶ ἐλάλησαν αὐτῷ τὸν λόγον τοῦ κυρίου σὺν πᾶσι τοῖς ἐν τῇ οἰκίᾳ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: And they spoke to him the word of the Lord with all the [ones] in the house of him.
pieces: And they shared the word of the Lord with him and with everyone in his household.

L.32: And they spoke the word of the Lord to him, with all those in his house.

R.32: Then Paul and Silas told the Lord's message to him and to everyone in his house.

decisions.choice: the word of the Lord: the message about the Lord Jesus
decisions.reason: The phrase is used through Acts for the gospel (8:25, 13:44, 15:35).

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: "the word of the Lord"
alternatives: some early manuscripts read "the word of God"
decisions.reason: A few early manuscripts have "of God". The sense hardly changes. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the Lord's message
decisions.reason: Readable says what the word was, as at 6:2.

decisions.choice: Paul and Silas
decisions.reason: Readable names the speakers.

records.source: καὶ παραλαβὼν αὐτοὺς ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ὥρᾳ τῆς νυκτὸς ἔλουσεν ἀπὸ τῶν πληγῶν, καὶ ἐβαπτίσθη αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ αὐτοῦ πάντες παραχρῆμα, ἀναγαγών τε αὐτοὺς εἰς τὸν οἶκον παρέθηκεν τράπεζαν καὶ ἠγαλλιάσατο πανοικεὶ πεπιστευκὼς τῷ θεῷ.
records.gloss: And having taken them in that the hour of the night he washed [them] from the wounds, and was baptized he and the [ones] of him all immediately, \v 34 having brought up and them into the house he set before [them] a table, and rejoiced with all the household having believed in the God.
pieces: Even at that hour of the night he took them and bathed their wounds, and straightaway he was baptized together with all his family.
Leading them up into his house, he spread a table for them, and the whole household rejoiced with him, now that he had believed in God.

L.33: And taking them in that hour of the night, he washed [them] from their wounds, and he was baptized at once, he and all his [household];
L.34: and bringing them up into the house, he set a table [before them], and he rejoiced with his whole household, having believed in God.

R.33: Even though it was the middle of the night, the jailer took Paul and Silas and washed their wounds. Then he and all his family were baptized right away.
R.34: He took Paul and Silas up into his house and gave them a meal. He and everyone in his house were full of joy, because he now believed in God.

decisions.choice: washed from their wounds, then was baptized: two washings
decisions.reason: He washes the blood from their backs, and then he himself is washed in baptism. The text sets the two acts side by side in the same hour.

decisions.choice: with his whole household: they rejoiced together, and the household also believed
decisions.reason: The word for the whole household may go with "rejoiced" or with "having believed". The participle is singular, about the jailer, but 16:31-33 show the word was spoken to all of them and all were baptized.

decisions.choice: brought them up into the house: the family lived above or beside the prison
decisions.reason: Jailers commonly lived at the prison. "Set a table" means he served them a meal.

decisions.choice: having believed in God: having come to faith in God
alternatives: having always believed in some god
decisions.reason: The perfect tense speaks of a lasting change. For a Gentile, believing in the Lord Jesus (16:31) meant believing in the one God.

decisions.choice: spread a table for them (B); gave them a meal (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture; Readable says what it meant.

decisions.choice: all his family
decisions.reason: The Greek says "all his", meaning his household, as the meaning note on 16:31 explains.

records.source: Ἡμέρας δὲ γενομένης ἀπέστειλαν οἱ στρατηγοὶ τοὺς ῥαβδούχους λέγοντες· Ἀπόλυσον τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐκείνους.
records.gloss: Day then having come sent the magistrates the rod-bearers saying, Release the men those.
pieces: In the morning the magistrates sent their lictors with the order, "Let those men go."

L.35: And when it was day, the magistrates sent the rod-bearers, saying, "Release those men."

R.35: The next morning the city officials sent their officers to the jailer with an order: "Let those men go free."

decisions.choice: the rod-bearers: the lictors, attendants who carried the magistrates' rods
decisions.reason: Roman magistrates were escorted by lictors, who carried bundles of rods as the sign of their power to punish. In a colony the two chief magistrates each had lictors. They had probably carried out the beating of 16:22-23.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the magistrates simply send the order
alternatives: Codex Bezae adds that the magistrates met in the marketplace and, remembering the earthquake, were afraid
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae and some related witnesses give a reason for the release. The shorter text gives none. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: those men: Paul and Silas
decisions.reason: The order concerns the two who were beaten and jailed the day before.

decisions.choice: lictors
decisions.reason: Balanced uses the Roman title, explained in the meaning note; Literal says what the Greek word means, rod-bearers.

decisions.choice: officers
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain word for the magistrates' attendants.

decisions.choice: to the jailer
decisions.reason: Readable says to whom the order went, as 16:36 shows.

records.heading: Roman citizens released

records.source: ἀπήγγειλεν δὲ ὁ δεσμοφύλαξ τοὺς λόγους τούτους πρὸς τὸν Παῦλον, ὅτι Ἀπέσταλκαν οἱ στρατηγοὶ ἵνα ἀπολυθῆτε· νῦν οὖν ἐξελθόντες πορεύεσθε ἐν εἰρήνῃ.
records.gloss: Reported then the jailer the words these to the Paul, that, Have sent the magistrates that you may be released; now therefore having come out go in peace.
pieces: The jailer passed the message on to Paul: "The magistrates have sent orders for your release. So come out now, and go in peace."

L.36: And the jailer reported these words to Paul: "The magistrates have sent [word] that you may be released. So now come out [and] go in peace."

R.36: The jailer told Paul, "The city officials have sent word that you can go free. So come out now and go in peace."

decisions.choice: go in peace: a farewell with a blessing
decisions.reason: The words are a common Jewish farewell (Luke 7:50, 8:48). From the jailer, now a believer, they are a wish for their good.

decisions.choice: you: plural, Paul and Silas
decisions.reason: The jailer speaks to Paul, but the verb is plural.

decisions.choice: the city officials
decisions.reason: Readable uses the plain description chosen at 16:20.

records.source: ὁ δὲ Παῦλος ἔφη πρὸς αὐτούς· Δείραντες ἡμᾶς δημοσίᾳ ἀκατακρίτους, ἀνθρώπους Ῥωμαίους ὑπάρχοντας, ἔβαλαν εἰς φυλακήν· καὶ νῦν λάθρᾳ ἡμᾶς ἐκβάλλουσιν;
records.gloss: But Paul was saying to them, Having beaten us publicly uncondemned, men Romans being, they threw [us] into prison, and now secretly us they throw out?
pieces: But Paul told them, "We are Roman citizens, and they beat us in front of everyone without condemning us in any court, and threw us into prison. Are they now going to send us away in secret?

L.37: But Paul said to them, "Having beaten us publicly, uncondemned, [though we are] Roman men, they threw [us] into prison, and now are they throwing us out secretly?

R.37: But Paul said to the officers, "We are Roman citizens. The officials beat us in front of everyone, but they never held a trial to show that we had done anything wrong. Then they threw us into prison. Do they now want to send us away secretly?

decisions.choice: beaten uncondemned, though Romans: a grave breach of Roman law
decisions.reason: Roman law from the Porcian laws onward forbade beating a Roman citizen, and above all without a trial. Cicero's speeches against Verres show how serious it was to treat a citizen so. Paul makes the same claim before a beating in Jerusalem (22:25-29).

decisions.choice: us, Romans: Silas also was a Roman citizen
decisions.reason: Paul speaks in the plural throughout, and the magistrates fear because "they" are Romans (16:38).

decisions.choice: uncondemned: without a trial and verdict
decisions.reason: The word means not condemned by a court. The magistrates had punished them without hearing their case.

decisions.choice: to them: to the lictors, and the jailer
decisions.reason: The lictors carry Paul's words back (16:38), so they were there with the jailer.

decisions.choice: the officers
decisions.reason: Readable names whom Paul spoke to, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: Roman citizens
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what being Roman meant here: citizenship, with its legal rights.

records.source: οὐ γάρ, ἀλλὰ ἐλθόντες αὐτοὶ ἡμᾶς ἐξαγαγέτωσαν.
records.gloss: No indeed, but having come themselves us let them bring out.
pieces: Certainly not! Let them come in person and lead us out."

L.37: No indeed! But let them come themselves and bring us out."

R.37: No! They must come here themselves and walk us out of the prison."

decisions.choice: let them bring us out: a public sign that they had done nothing wrong
decisions.reason: Luke does not give Paul's reason. Being led out by the magistrates would show the city that the missionaries were innocent, and it may have protected the new believers they left behind (16:40).

decisions.choice: no indeed: a strong refusal
decisions.reason: The two little words together reject the idea outright.

records.source: ἀπήγγειλαν δὲ τοῖς στρατηγοῖς οἱ ῥαβδοῦχοι τὰ ῥήματα ταῦτα· ἐφοβήθησαν δὲ ἀκούσαντες ὅτι Ῥωμαῖοί εἰσιν, καὶ ἐλθόντες παρεκάλεσαν αὐτούς, καὶ ἐξαγαγόντες ἠρώτων ἀπελθεῖν ἀπὸ τῆς πόλεως.
records.gloss: Reported then to the magistrates the rod-bearers the words these; they were afraid then having heard that Romans they are, \v 39 and having come they appealed to them, and having brought [them] out they were asking [them] to go away from the city.
pieces: The lictors carried these words back to the magistrates, who were frightened to hear that the men were Roman citizens.
They came and pleaded with them, and after leading them out, they kept asking them to leave the city.

L.38: And the rod-bearers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that they were Romans,
L.39: and they came and appealed to them, and bringing [them] out, they asked [them] to go away from the city.

R.38: The officers told the city officials what Paul had said. The officials were afraid when they heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens.
R.39: So they came and said they were sorry. They led them out of the prison and asked them to leave the city.

decisions.choice: they were afraid: they could be punished for what they had done
decisions.reason: Officials who beat a Roman citizen without trial could lose their office or face trial themselves, and the colony itself could be punished.

decisions.choice: appealed to them: spoke to them gently, to make peace
decisions.reason: The verb can mean to urge, comfort or appeal. Here it is the magistrates' attempt to calm the men they had wronged.

decisions.choice: were asking: they asked more than once
decisions.reason: The imperfect suggests repeated asking.

decisions.choice: SBLGNT: the shorter account
alternatives: Codex Bezae adds that the magistrates came with many friends and admitted they had not known the men were innocent
decisions.reason: Codex Bezae expands this verse, making the magistrates plead more fully. Reviewers should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: said they were sorry
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of the meaning note in plain words. It is a little more definite than the Greek.

decisions.choice: Roman citizens
decisions.reason: As at 16:37.

records.source: ἐξελθόντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς φυλακῆς εἰσῆλθον πρὸς τὴν Λυδίαν, καὶ ἰδόντες παρεκάλεσαν τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ ἐξῆλθαν.
records.gloss: Having gone out then from the prison they went in to the Lydia, and having seen they encouraged the brothers and departed.
pieces: So they came out of the prison and went to Lydia. They saw the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} and encouraged them, and then they set out.

L.40: And going out of the prison, they went in to Lydia, and seeing the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, they encouraged [them] and departed.

R.40: Paul and Silas left the prison and went to Lydia's house. They met with the {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}} there and encouraged them. Then they left Philippi.

decisions.choice: the brothers: the believers at Philippi, men and women
decisions.reason: The church met at Lydia's house; it included her household and the jailer's, among others.

decisions.choice: they: Paul and Silas; the narrator does not say "we"
decisions.reason: The "we" of 16:10-17 does not return here. It returns at Philippi in 20:5-6, so the narrator may have stayed in the city.

decisions.choice: encouraged: urged and comforted
decisions.reason: The verb means to call alongside, to strengthen with words.

decisions.choice: brothers and sisters, with "brothers" as the alternative
decisions.reason: The word takes in all the believers, as the meaning note explains.

decisions.choice: Lydia's house; Philippi
decisions.reason: Readable says where they went and what they left.
